documents.t: The WiFi LoRa 32 is a well-known IoT development board created by Heltec Automation. Since its release in 2017, it has been popular among developers and makers. The new V3 version keeps the same pin layout as the V2 and continues to support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), LoRa, and an OLED display. This board is ideal for applications in smart cities, smart farming, home automation, industrial control, security systems, wireless metering, and general IoT development.

Equipped with an ESP32-S3FN8 microprocessor, featuring a dual-core Xtensa® 32-bit LX7 CPU, five-stage pipeline, and clock speed up to 240 MHz. Integrated SX1262 LoRa chip for long-range wireless communication. USB Type-C interface with built-in voltage regulation, ESD protection, short-circuit protection, RF shielding, and other safety features. Includes an SH1.25-2 battery connector and a built-in lithium battery management system that supports charging, discharging, overcharge protection, battery level monitoring, and automatic power switching between USB and battery. Features a 0.96-inch OLED display (128×64 resolution) for showing debug info, battery status, and more. Supports Wi-Fi, LoRa, and Bluetooth connectivity. Comes with a built-in 2.4GHz metal spring antenna for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and a reserved IPEX (U.FL) port for LoRa. Uses the CP2102 USB-to-serial chip, making it easy to upload code and view debug output. Compatible with the Arduino development environment for quick and flexible programming. Designed with a high-quality RF circuit and low power consumption for efficient operation.

Parameters Description Master Chip ESP32-S3FN8 (Xtensa®32-bit lx7 dual core processor) LoRa Node Chip SX1262 USB to Serial Chip CP2102 Frequency 470-510MHz, 863-928MHz Max. TX Power 21±1dBm Max. Receiving sensitivity -134dBm@SF12 BW=125KHz Wi-Fi 802.11 b/g/n, up to 150Mbps Bluetooth Bluetooth 5 (LE) Hardware Resource 7 * ADC, 2 * ADC2, 7 * Touch,3 * UART, 2 * I2C, 2 * SPI, etc.. Memory 384KB ROM, 512KB SRAM, 16KB RTC SRAM, 8MB SiP Flash Interface Type-C USB, 2 * 1.25 battery interface, LoRa ANT(IPEX1.0), 2 * 18 * 2.54 Header Pin Battery 3.7V lithium battery power supply and charging Operating Temperature -20 ~ 70 ℃ Dimensions 50.2 * 25.5* 10.2 mm

Install Meshtastic or MeshCore firmware and recover devices after failed updates.

Applicable models: N30, N32, N32 Plus, N33, N35, N35 Plus Connect your device to a computer using a USB data cable. Open the official Meshtastic Web Flasher using Chrome or Edge. Select the firmware target that matches your actual hardware version. Choose the firmware version and follow the on-screen instructions. Wait for the installation to finish before disconnecting the device. N30, N32, and N33 use Heltec V3 hardware. N35 is available with Heltec V3 or V4 hardware, so make sure you select the correct version. Back up important configuration and channel information before performing a full flash erase. Related resources: Meshtastic Web Flasher

After updating, restart the device, connect it to the Meshtastic app, and check that LoRa communication and GPS positioning are working correctly. Do not install Heltec V3 firmware on the N39. documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 MeshCore firmware is available for various LoRa hardware platforms, including selected Heltec and Seeed devices. documents.t: Connect your device, configure Meshtastic, and resolve basic communication issues.

Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 Yes. Meshtastic devices communicate with other compatible nodes through LoRa radio without relying on cellular service or internet access. You can connect a compatible device to your smartphone through Bluetooth and use the Meshtastic app to send and receive messages. The devices must be within radio communication range, either directly or through compatible mesh nodes. Related resources: Getting Started Guide
documents.s: Can Meshtastic devices work without Wi-Fi, cellular service, or the internet?

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 Power on your device and enable Bluetooth on your smartphone. Download and open the Meshtastic app. Navigate to the device connection screen and select your device. Follow the pairing instructions and enter the Bluetooth PIN if prompted. Configure the correct LoRa region before transmitting messages. If your device does not appear, restart it and make sure it is running compatible Meshtastic firmware. Related resources: Getting Started Guide
documents.s: How do I connect my N30, N35, N37, or N39 to my smartphone?

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 A successful Bluetooth connection does not necessarily mean the LoRa radio link is working. Make sure both devices have matching LoRa settings, including the region, modem preset, and frequency slot. For private channels, the channel settings and encryption keys must also match. Check the antenna connections and test the devices at a short distance in an open area. If communication still fails, verify that both devices are running compatible firmware and check whether either device reports a LoRa initialization error.
documents.s: Why can my devices connect to the app but not exchange messages?

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 Yes. Different Meshnology models can communicate with one another when they use compatible Meshtastic firmware, matching radio settings, and supported regional frequencies. For example, an N30 can exchange messages with an N37 or N39 when the devices are configured correctly. However, Meshtastic and MeshCore use different communication protocols. Devices running these two firmware systems cannot directly exchange native mesh messages without a compatible bridging solution.
documents.s: Can different Meshnology device models communicate with each other?

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 You can configure and test a single Meshtastic device using the smartphone app. However, sending messages over LoRa requires another compatible node within radio range. If an existing Meshtastic network is available in your area, one device may be enough to join it. Otherwise, we recommend starting with two devices to test communication and build your own local network.

Applicable models: N30鈥揘39, ThinkNode M3, M7, M9 The appropriate LoRa frequency depends on your country or region and the hardware version of your device. The United States commonly uses the 902鈥?28MHz band for Meshtastic, while European Meshtastic configurations generally use the 868MHz region. Choose a device and antenna suitable for your local radio regulations, and configure the correct region in your firmware before transmitting. A device advertised with a broad frequency range is not necessarily optimized or certified for every frequency within that range.

Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 The actual communication range depends on terrain, antenna performance, installation height, obstacles, radio interference, and LoRa settings. An open area with a clear line of sight generally provides better communication conditions than an indoor environment or a densely built urban area. There is no single guaranteed communication distance for every deployment. For the most reliable results, test your devices in the environment where you intend to use them.
documents.s: How far can my Meshnology device communicate?

documents.t: Applicable models: N37, N37E, N39, ThinkNode M7 Yes. Compatible LoRa devices can be used to build local mesh networks for outdoor communication, GPS tracking, and monitoring. For larger deployments, consider installing compatible relay nodes at elevated locations with suitable power supplies, antenna positioning, and weather protection. The N37, N37E, and N39 support GPS positioning, while the ThinkNode M7 provides Ethernet and PoE connectivity for compatible gateway applications. Network design should be based on site conditions, coverage testing, and the expected number of users and devices. Related resources: N37 N37E N39

documents.t: Applicable models: N37, N37E, N39 The N37 and N37E platforms support solar power input, and the Heltec V4-based N39 provides a solar input interface. For outdoor installations, use compatible solar panels, suitable battery protection, and appropriate charging and power-management components. Solar charging performance depends on panel output, available sunlight, device power consumption, and the specific hardware configuration. Please refer to the product鈥檚 technical documentation before connecting an external power source. Related resources: N37 N37E N39 Meshnology Wiki

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39 Weather resistance varies depending on the product and enclosure design. A protective case does not automatically make a device waterproof or suitable for prolonged exposure to rain, snow, or high humidity. Unless the specific product documentation states a verified ingress protection rating, we recommend using an appropriate weatherproof enclosure for permanent outdoor installations. Make sure antenna connections, charging ports, and cable entry points are properly protected.

Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N36, N37, N37E, N39, ThinkNode M9 The right device depends on your intended application. N30: A compact Meshtastic device with a 1100mAh battery, suitable for beginners and everyday communication. N32 / N33: Heltec V3-based devices with 3000mAh batteries, suitable for portable messaging and mesh networking. N35 / N35 Plus: Devices with 3000mAh batteries and Heltec V3 or V4 hardware options. N36: An nRF52840-based device designed for low-power wireless communication. N37: A device featuring GPS and an OLED display. N37E: A GPS-enabled device featuring a low-power E-Ink display. N39: A Heltec V4-based device featuring GPS and hardware expansion capabilities. ThinkNode M9: A standalone communication device with a physical keyboard, display, and GPS. Choose your device based on battery capacity, display type, GPS requirements, firmware compatibility, and intended use. Related resources: N35 N37 N37E N39 ThinkNode M9

documents.t: Applicable models: N30, N32, N33, N35, N35 Plus The N30 features a 1100mAh battery, making it a compact option for portable communication. The N32 and N33 both use the Heltec V3 platform and feature 3000mAh batteries, but they have different enclosure designs. The N35 is available with Heltec V3 or V4 hardware options and includes a 3000mAh battery. Please check the selected product variant and package contents before purchasing. Related resources: N35

documents.t: Applicable models: N35, N35 Plus The N35 enclosure is designed to accommodate compatible Heltec V3 and V4 boards. Always select the firmware that matches your actual hardware version. Related resources: N35

documents.t: Applicable models: N37, N37E Both devices are based on the Seeed Wio Tracker L1 platform and feature an nRF52840 processor, SX1262 LoRa radio, and GNSS positioning. The N37 features a 1.3-inch OLED display, while the N37E uses a 2.13-inch E-Ink display. The OLED display is suitable for regular screen updates, while the E-Ink display is designed for low-power applications involving primarily static information. The two models require firmware that matches their respective display configurations. Related resources: N37 N37E

documents.t: Applicable models: N39 Yes. The Meshnology N39 is equipped with GPS functionality and is based on the Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V4 platform. With compatible firmware and proper configuration, the N39 can obtain location information and share its position with other nodes over a Meshtastic network. GPS reception depends on satellite visibility and environmental conditions. For better positioning performance, use the device in an open outdoor area. Related resources: N39
documents.s: Does the Meshnology N39 have GPS?

documents.t: Applicable models: N37, N37E, N39 Yes. All three models support GPS positioning without requiring cellular service or an internet connection. When configured with compatible Meshtastic firmware, they can share location information with other nodes through LoRa communication. To view another device鈥檚 position remotely, a functioning radio connection must be available, either directly or through compatible mesh nodes. GPS positioning and LoRa communication are separate functions. Obtaining a GPS fix does not automatically guarantee that another node can receive the location information. Related resources: N37 N37E N39

documents.t: Applicable models: ThinkNode M9 Yes. The ThinkNode M9 features a physical keyboard and a 2.4-inch LCD display, allowing users to compose and read messages directly on the device. It also features GPS, a magnetic compass, an LR1110 LoRa radio, and a 2300mAh battery. The M9 is suitable for users who want a standalone communication device without relying on a smartphone for everyday messaging. Please select the appropriate firmware and regional frequency version when purchasing. Related resources: ThinkNode M9

documents.t: Applicable models: ThinkNode M7 The ThinkNode M7 is available in separate Meshtastic and LoRaWAN versions. The Meshtastic version is designed for mesh networking, while the LoRaWAN version is intended for LoRaWAN applications. These two systems cannot operate simultaneously on the same device. The M7 features Ethernet and PoE connectivity, making it suitable for compatible gateway applications. Please select the appropriate firmware version and regional frequency when purchasing.

documents.t: Applicable models: ThinkNode M3 Yes. The ThinkNode M3 includes environmental and motion-sensing capabilities, including temperature, humidity, and accelerometer sensors. It also supports GNSS positioning and LoRa communication. Available sensor functions, data reporting intervals, and remote monitoring capabilities depend on the installed firmware and device configuration.

If the device still does not appear, check whether your computer can detect it through USB. If necessary, reinstall the correct firmware for your hardware version. Check that the antenna and RF connections are secure. If the display, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi functions work but the LoRa error remains, the radio subsystem may require further diagnosis. Please contact technical support with your firmware version, hardware revision, and a photo of the error message. Related resources: N39 Heltec V4 Expansion Kit

If your firmware does not support display rotation, we recommend restoring a compatible Meshtastic firmware version or checking the MeshCore community for a verified firmware update. Do not repeatedly install unrelated firmware builds, as this may introduce additional compatibility issues. Related resources: MeshCore Web Flasher Meshtastic Web Flasher

A USB drive named 鈥淭racker L1鈥?should appear on your computer. Download the correct UF2 firmware file for your device and follow the official flashing instructions. If the device cannot enter DFU mode, the bootloader may need to be restored. If the device remains unresponsive after recovery, contact technical support for further assistance. Related resources: Meshtastic Web Flasher Meshnology Wiki

documents.t: Applicable models: Mesh Pocket M1 First, check the battery level and charging status. Restart the device using the manufacturer鈥檚 documented procedure and check whether Bluetooth connectivity is restored. If the device remains stuck on the startup screen or cannot be detected by the Meshtastic app, contact technical support with your order number, device information, and a short video showing the issue. Do not open the battery enclosure or install firmware intended for a different Heltec board.

Restart the device, disconnect any previous Bluetooth connections, and try pairing again through the appropriate app. If the problem persists, connect the device to a computer and check whether it can be detected through USB. For touchscreen models, make sure the firmware supports the installed display and expansion hardware. If the device remains unresponsive, contact technical support before performing a full flash erase. Related resources: Heltec V4 Expansion Kit

documents.t: Applicable models: N37, N37E, N39 Make sure the GPS antenna is correctly connected and positioning is enabled in your device settings. Move the device outdoors to an area with a clear view of the sky and allow sufficient time for satellite acquisition. Check the GPS status in the Meshtastic app. If you want to share your location with other nodes, confirm that position reporting is enabled. If the device still cannot obtain a GPS fix outdoors, contact technical support with your product model, hardware revision, firmware version, and GPS status information. Related resources: N37 N37E N39

documents.t: The M19 LR2021 Video Device (Multimedia LoRa Dev Terminal) is a multimedia LoRa development board built around an ESP32-S3R8 dual-core MCU (up to 240 MHz, 8 MB OPI PSRAM + 16 MB Flash) and the fourth-generation LR2021 LoRa transceiver. Compared with OLED-only boards, M19 adds a 1.22-inch 240×240 colour LCD, a DVP camera, MicroSD storage, and LoRa image / short-video transmission, while keeping full-band Wi-Fi 4 + BLE 5.0 + dual-band LoRa (Sub-1 GHz and 2.4 GHz). Local UI navigation is handled by the on-board BOOT key and an ADC five-way key (up / down / left / right / center). Typical uses include field video snapshot over LoRa, portable inspection terminals, outdoor GNSS-assisted nodes, and multimode IoT prototyping. M19 uses the Meshnology Web Flasher. No separate desktop flashing utility is required. Preparation​ Hardware: M19 development board, Type-C USB data cable (must support data transfer) Software environment: Use a Chrome or Edge browser (must support Web Serial). No additional software installation is required. Access the tool: Open https://meshnology-flasher.pages.dev/ Serial port not detected If your computer cannot detect the device when clicking Choose serial port, press and hold the BOOT button on the development board, then press and release the RST button. Keep holding BOOT until the computer recognizes the serial port. You can release BOOT once the device is connected. Flashing steps​ 1. Select chip type​ In the Connect device panel on the left, select ESP32 family from the CHIP FAMILY dropdown menu. If you are connecting an ESP32-S3 device such as the M19, the tool will automatically detect the chip model. 2. Select firmware​ Choose one of the following two methods depending on your needs: Method A: Local upload (recommended) Single merged .bin: Click browse from your computer or drag and drop the merged .bin file into the dashed box. This is the fastest method. Multiple files + offsets: Open the Multiple files + offsets tab, add the bootloader, partition table, application files, and fill in the correct offset addresses. Method B: Pick a device (official online firmware, including MeshCore) Use this method to flash cloud-hosted firmware such as MeshCore (no local .bin required). Click the Pick a device tab. In DEVICE, select M19 Meshnology LCD (MeshCore, ESP32-S3) (latest version, for example 1.0.0). The tool automatically matches the MeshCore firmware image and recommended flash parameters. Method Typical use Method A — Local upload Factory / peripheral demos from M19_Demo_Details.rar, or your own *.merged.bin Method B — Pick a device Official MeshCore firmware for M19 (online) 3. Choose serial port​ Click the green Choose serial port button on the left. In the browser serial port selection window, select the corresponding device port (usually displayed as USB JTAG/serial debug unit or COMx) and click Connect. 4. Configure flash parameters (optional)​ In the Flash parameters section: Default: Keep MODE, FREQUENCY, and FLASH SIZE all set to Auto. Manual specification: If Auto fails, manually select: MODE: DIO FREQUENCY: 80 MHz FLASH SIZE: 16 MB 5. Start flashing​ Click the blue Flash single file button at the bottom to start flashing. Observe the TERMINAL window below; it will show erase and write progress (for example, Writing at 0x... (xx%)). Wait for the progress bar to reach 100%. When the terminal finally displays Done. and [esptool] board reset, the firmware has been written successfully. The device will automatically reset and reboot. If it does not reboot automatically, manually press the RST button on the development board to complete the flashing process.

Programme Description​ The M19 demo firmware is a comprehensive factory test and function demonstration firmware developed for the ESP32-S3R8 (16MB Flash + 8MB OPI PSRAM) development board. The UI uses an LVGL 8.4.x left-right page-turning (Tileview) design. The pages include: Detect → Status → WiFi&BLE → LoRa Six States → LoRa Image Transmission → Camera Preview. It supports page turning and function switching via the BOOT key and ADC five-way key, and includes battery ADC, RGB LED, and deep-sleep standby functions. Boot Process​ After power-on, the device automatically runs the initialization self-test process and stays on the Detect page by default. This page displays whether peripherals such as LCD / SD / Camera / GPS / LoRa / WiFi / BLE were initialized successfully. UI Page Overview​ Page Function Description Detect Displays whether LCD / SD / Camera / GPS / LoRa / WiFi / BLE were initialized successfully Status Runtime status summary (including battery voltage, GPS positioning information, latitude/longitude/satellite count, device SN, etc.) WiFi&BLE WiFi STA (default SSID/connection status/IP/RSSI), BLE peripheral name/connection status/received packet preview; WiFi/BLE are actually loaded only when entering this page LoRa Six States Includes six working states: SubG_RX / SubG_TX / SubG_CW / 2G4_RX / 2G4_TX / 2G4_CW LoRa Image Sub-G FLRC image transmission (JPEG), supports TX/RX, short video, broadcast listen-only RX Camera DVP RGB565 camera preview (FB in PSRAM) Key Operations and System Mechanisms​ BOOT key (short press): Next page; short press on the LoRa page switches modes. ADC five-way key (up/down/left/right/center): Controls page turning / LoRa state switching / TX-RX-shooting on the image page, etc. Power/deep-sleep mechanism: The device automatically enters deep-sleep mode after about 10 minutes of inactivity; long-pressing the BOOT key can trigger the shutdown/standby path. LoRa Test Instructions​ Item Parameter/Description LoRa Module LR2021 (supports Sub-G and 2.4G) Working Modes Key cycles through Sub-G / 2.4G RX, TX, CW (six states in total) Image Transmission Sub-G FLRC image transmission (JPEG, esp_new_jpeg) Critical resource management SPI bus sharing: LCD / LoRa / SD share the same bus. In LoRa TX/CW mode or during image transmission, the system automatically freezes LVGL and yields the shared SPI to the RF to prevent display corruption. Memory and DMA staggering: Arduino internal RAM is relatively tight. WiFi, Camera DMA, and BLE need to be staggered; when entering the LoRa/Image/Camera pages, the system automatically suspends WiFi+BLE to free up contiguous internal DMA blocks. Quick Operation Reference​ Operation Effect Power on Automatic initialization, enters the Detect page Page turning (Detect → Status → WiFi&BLE → LoRa → Image → Camera) Left/right five-way key / BOOT short press Up/down five-way key / BOOT short press (on LoRa page) Switch among six states (RX/TX/CW, etc.) Center key / BOOT short press (on image page) Control TX/RX start/stop, pause/shoot Serial monitor (115200) View boot logs and initialization status of each peripheral Common troubleshooting BLE error HLI / IWDT: Confirm that the code includes esp32-hal-alloc-ble-mem.h and that a full rebuild has been performed. WiFi NO_MEM + LCD SPI failure: Caused by internal RAM fragmentation. Do not forcibly enable WiFi and Camera DMA at the same time; follow the system's lazy-loading mechanism. Q1. Which development environments are supported? A：Supports common ESP32 development tools such as the Arduino IDE, PlatformIO, and ESP-IDF. Q2. How to optimise LoRa transmission parameters? A：Configure Meshtastic settings according to statutory frequency band allocations, SF (spread factor) and Bandwidth. Q3. How to use GNSS? A：Connect the GNSS module via the SH1.25-8Pin interface and utilise the corresponding firmware for expansion. Q4. 2.4GHz antenna A：The default 2.4G FPC antenna is located on the side of the plastic screen bracket. If you wish to use the 2.4G antenna connected via IPEX, you must remove the inductor marked as ① in the diagram below and add a 0-ohm resistor (or other conductive metal or cable) at the position marked as ② to connect to the IPEX interface. Q5. My screw looks a bit odd? A：This area incorporates a 2.4 GHz FPC antenna. To prevent compromising its performance, custom-made plastic screws have been employed here. This is why they look different from ordinary screws. When disassembly is required, simply press down gently with a screwdriver and turn. Q6. What type of battery socket is it? A：You can find this type of socket by searching for "SH1.25 x 2". Q7. Are Heltec V3 and V4 compatible? A：They are compatible in most cases. As V4 utilises the same series of chips as V3, features identical OLED displays, and possesses virtually identical pin layouts, V3 and V4 units are interchangeable in most scenarios. However, due to increased transmission power, the transmission power settings within certain code may no longer correspond directly to the actual output. Q8. Code upload failed A：Please try the following steps： Please try using a different USB cable. Enter bootloader mode. There are two methods to enter this mode.： Press and hold the PRG button, connect the USB-C cable, then release the PRG button. Connect the USB-C cable, press and hold the PRG button, press the RST button once, then release the PRG button. Q9. Why are there no soldered resistors at the 868 and 915 markings? Which frequency band does my device actually support? A：It indicates simultaneous support for both the 868 MHz and 915 MHz frequency bands. In the initial design, we developed two separate hardware versions to achieve optimal radio frequency performance. However, through subsequent debugging, we successfully unified the hardware for both the 868 MHz and 915 MHz bands while maintaining excellent radio frequency characteristics.

The Visual Line Tracking Demo implements the movement of the racing car within the track based on a purely visual method, with guiding lines in the middle of the track assisting the car to stay within the track.

To achieve the above function, three main modules are needed: Visual Input Environment Perception Motion Control These modules interact as follows: The Visual Input module obtains images of the real world (or simulated world) and passes them to the environment perception module. The Environment Perception module analyzes the position of the racing car on the track and sends relevant information to the motion control module. The Motion Control module calculates motion control commands based on the car’s position and sends them to the chassis for execution.

The SD card provides a stable local storage solution for collected audio-visual data and AI model files. Notably, the embedded machine learning capabilities of the ESP32-S3 chip synergise perfectly with the board's audio-visual capture hardware. Developers can directly undertake intelligent image recognition, voice wake-up and recognition, and edge AI inference tasks without requiring complex external modules. Indeed, the ESP32S3 Mini Module series represents the ideal choice for makers, electronics engineers, and AI beginners embarking on intelligent voice and visual AI projects.

Programme Description​ Arduino IDE Supplementary configuration​ The ESP32's PSRAM refers to the external PSRAM (Pseudo-Static Random Access Memory) on the ESP32 chip, which provides additional memory space to augment the available memory of the ESP32 system. Within the ESP32 system, PSRAM serves the following primary purposes: Expanding available RAM: The ESP32's built-in RAM is limited, particularly for applications requiring substantial memory such as image processing or audio processing, where the internal RAM may prove insufficient. Utilising PSRAM enables the expansion of the ESP32's available RAM to meet the demands of such applications. Accelerating memory access: Whilst PSRAM is external memory and thus slower than internal RAM, it can serve as cache or temporary storage to expedite memory access and data processing. Storing buffers: For applications requiring substantial buffers—such as network buffers or audio buffers—PSRAM provides ample storage capacity to prevent memory shortages. For the purposes of this tutorial, you must enable the PSRAM feature within the Arduino IDE to ensure the camera functions correctly. Define hardware communication pins: Default configuration for XIAO ESP32S3 (with PSRAM) camera, SD card select pin = 21, supports custom modification Configure core camera parameters: Set 20MHz clock, UXGA frame size, JPEG format; automatically adjusts JPEG quality and frame buffer based on PSRAM Camera module self-test: Executes camera initialisation, prints success/error codes via serial port to verify hardware functionality Initialise SD card: Mounts SD card using GPIO21 as chip select, prints mount success/failure via serial port to validate storage module Detect SD card information: Identifies and outputs SD card type via serial port; terminates storage process if no valid card is present Mark SD Card Ready: Flag status once SD card is normal; photo capture only triggers when both camera and SD card are ready Configure timed photography: Default 60-second interval, triggered by millisecond-accurate timing, supports adjustable capture frequency Generate incrementing filenames: Automatically creates files like /image1.jpg, prevents overwriting, supports continuous storage Capture JPEG images: Retrieves camera image buffer upon trigger, extracts complete image data Save images to SD card: Writes images to corresponding files, serial port prints success/failure status to confirm storage validity Release image buffer: Frees frame buffer after saving to prevent memory leaks and ensure stable operation Incremental photo sequence numbering: Updates file sequence numbers to guarantee unique filenames, supporting uninterrupted continuous capture and storage. Function Overview​ Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is an energy-optimised variant of traditional Bluetooth technology, designed primarily for short-range, low-bandwidth wireless data transmission involving small data volumes. BLE employs a distinct operating mechanism from conventional Bluetooth, remaining inactive most of the time rather than maintaining a constant active state. It enters operational mode only when establishing connections and executing data transfers, spending the majority of its time in a low-power sleep state. Thanks to its unique low-power operating mode, BLE significantly reduces energy consumption. Across various practical use cases, its power consumption is approximately one per cent of that of traditional Bluetooth. BLE's characteristics make it particularly suitable for devices powered by button batteries, requiring long-term stable operation, and needing only to exchange small amounts of data periodically. BLE has extensive application scenarios, commonly found in healthcare devices, fitness equipment, various trackers, wireless beacons, security devices, and smart home products. Server and Client​ The ESP32S3 Mini Module development board supports flexible role switching, functioning either as a server or configurable for client operation. BLE Server Device: Its core function is to actively broadcast its presence signal for discovery and identification by neighbouring BLE devices. The server internally stores data resources accessible for reading and retrieval by client devices. BLE Client Device: Its core behaviour involves actively scanning for BLE devices within range. Upon detecting and matching a target server device, it initiates a connection request to establish a stable communication link, subsequently listening for or retrieving incoming data from the server device. This communication interaction between BLE servers and clients falls within the realm of peer-to-peer (P2P) communication, representing a fundamental and prevalent communication form within BLE technology. Core Definition of Data Transmission​ Attributes (data entries)Underlying data → ATT Protocol Underlying Commands / Packets → GATT AgreementHigh-Level Organisation / Transmission Rules → Ordered data transmission between BLE devices (sensor data, control commands, etc.), forming a complete logical closed loop for BLE data transfer. Deep sleep​ Programme Description​ In deep sleep mode, the ESP32 deactivates the CPU, most RAM, and all digital peripherals driven by the APB_CLK clock. Only the following components remain powered: RTC controller ULP coprocessor RTC fast memory RTC slow memory Wake-up Methods: Timer Wake-up: The ESP32 can be configured to automatically wake up after a specified time via a timer. Touchpad Interrupt Wake-up: The device can be awakened by touchpad activity, suitable for applications requiring user interaction. External Wake-up: The ESP32 can be awakened by external signals (such as button presses), ideal for low-power applications. ULP Coprocessor Activity Wake-up: The ULP coprocessor operates independently, monitoring specific conditions and waking the main CPU to conserve power. GPIO Wake-up: The device may be awakened by changes in GPIO pin states (high or low), offering flexibility for various sensors and peripherals. ‼️ Important Notice Should the ESP32S3 Mini Module enter sleep mode and require reprogramming, it must be placed into programming mode. Follow these steps: Disconnect the board's USB power supply (unplug the USB cable) to prevent operational errors during powered operation Press and hold the BOOT pin firmly (maintain pressure without releasing) Reinsert the USB cable to power the board (while still holding the BOOT pin down), maintaining pressure for 1-2 seconds Release the BOOT pin. The board will now enter programming mode, and the device will appear as online in the Arduino IDE interface Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer using a USB cable. Operational performance​ TimerWakeUP: Set the conversion value for microseconds to seconds, a 5-second sleep duration, and a dedicated storage area to record the number of device starts (sleep does not cause loss). Develop a function query to display the device wake-up cause via serial port (timed / external signal, etc.); Initiate serial port communication and wait for one second to ensure proper transmission; Start count incremented by one; serial port displays current start count. The function displays the reason for this wake-up, facilitating troubleshooting. Enable scheduled wake-up, set to automatically wake the device after 5 seconds; Serial port display hibernation settings, indicating imminent entry into deep hibernation; Refresh the serial port buffer to ensure all information is printed in full. The device enters deep sleep mode, after which the programme ceases operation. The main programme loop contains no additional functionality and performs no superfluous operations. Operational effect： ExternalWakeUP: Import the tool library, configure the wake-up pin GPIO33 and its parameters, with dedicated memory recording the number of starts (non-volatile during sleep); Initiate serial port communication and wait for one second to ensure proper transmission; Start count incremented by one; serial port displays current start count. Invoke function to print the reason for the device's wake-up via serial port (for debugging purposes). Default EXT0 mode enabled: GPIO33 high level wakes the device; Configure GPIO33: Disable pull-up, enable pull-down to prevent erratic level fluctuations causing unintended wake-up; If EXT0 is disabled, EXT1 mode shall be enabled, with GPIO33 high level triggering wake-up; Serial port prompt: Device is about to enter deep sleep mode; The device enters deep sleep mode, ceasing execution of subsequent programmes, and awaits a high-level signal on GPIO33 to awaken. Operational performance： Light_sleep​ Programme Description​ Introduction: Light Sleep Mode is a core low-power mode for the ESP32 series of chips, offering the dual advantages of high energy efficiency and rapid wake-up response. In this mode, the CPU core enters a suspended state to reduce power consumption, while RAM and certain peripherals remain powered to ensure the device can rapidly wake and respond when triggered by external events. Furthermore, Light Sleep Mode supports keeping WiFi and Bluetooth modules active, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring both low-power operation and the continuous maintenance of wireless communication connections. Wake-up methods: Timer Wake-up: Supports preset wake-up intervals, enabling automatic device activation upon reaching specified times to fulfil periodic task execution requirements. External Interrupt Wake-up: Responds to various external hardware interrupt signals for wake-up, with typical scenarios including button presses and external sensor triggers. Network Activity Wake-up: Responds to incoming network packets to awaken the device, eliminating the need for continuous active status and enhancing power efficiency in wireless communication scenarios. GPIO Wake-up: Allows designated GPIO pins to be configured as wake-up sources. When a pin experiences a state change or detects a specific signal, it triggers the device to awaken from light sleep. Note： Define two core parameters: the 10-second device light sleep duration and the control pin for the on-board LED, preparing for subsequent processes. Write an LED-specific task: illuminate the LED and print a prompt; maintain illumination for 1 second before extinguishing the LED and printing a prompt; automatically delete itself upon task completion to release resources. Configure wake-up functionality: Set up a 10-second timer-based wake-up function to automatically rouse the device from sleep at the designated time. Execute light sleep sequence: Print a sleep prompt via the serial port, then enter light sleep mode, operating at low power for 10 seconds. Trigger post-wakeup lighting task: Upon awakening, create and execute the LED control task to achieve a 1-second LED illumination followed by extinction. Prepare for next cycle: After completing the LED task, introduce a 1-second delay for process stabilisation before commencing the next "sleep - wake - lighting control" cycle. Achieving Periodic Low-Power Operation: The main loop contains no additional operations, continuously repeating the core process to implement periodic low-power lighting control. Operational performance​ Modem sleep mode（Modem_sleep）​ Programme Description​ Introduction: Modem Sleep Mode is a significant low-power mode for the ESP32, operating distinctly from Deep Sleep Mode. Its core optimisation targets the ESP32's WiFi/Bluetooth wireless communication modules. In this mode, the ESP32's WiFi and Bluetooth modules enter a dormant state to reduce power consumption, while the CPU core remains active. This approach significantly reduces the device's overall power consumption while retaining some wireless connectivity capability, balancing energy efficiency with fundamental operational requirements. Wake-up methods: Timer Wake-up: Devices automatically awaken upon reaching preset fixed durations or precise time points when conditions are met, requiring no external intervention. Primarily suited for periodic tasks (such as scheduled data collection or cyclical status reporting). External Interrupt Wake-up: The device responds to interrupt signals generated by external hardware to achieve wake-up. Trigger sources include button presses, sensor threshold activations, or external device level changes. This method offers real-time responsiveness, suitable for scenarios requiring rapid detection of external events. Task Wake-up: Within multi-tasking operating systems (e.g., FreeRTOS), other ready tasks trigger the wake-up of designated dormant tasks via communication mechanisms such as semaphores, message queues, or event groups. This suits scenarios requiring inter-task coordination and on-demand execution (e.g., waking a foreground display task upon completion of background data processing). Network Activity Wake-up: The device responds to incoming network events—such as incoming network packets or connection requests—to awaken itself. This avoids maintaining the wireless module in high-power active mode continuously, balancing energy efficiency with the real-time nature of network communication. It is suitable for scenarios involving receiving cloud commands or network data exchange. Enable ESP32 modem sleep mode, print a prompt, and conserve WiFi module power. Main loop first prints "Program running", then delays for 5 seconds (maintaining WiFi power-saving). Disable modem sleep mode, print a prompt, and wake the WiFi module to active state. Check WiFi connection status, printing either "Connection maintained" or "Connection lost". Delay for 5 seconds (maintaining WiFi activity), then re-enable modem sleep mode and print a prompt. Continuously loop to implement a "WiFi power-saving 5 seconds - active 5 seconds" periodic cycle, balancing energy conservation with status monitoring. Programme Description​ 💡NOTE It is not recommended to perform video encoding and file export operations directly on the MCU hardware platform. The core reasons are as follows: at present, video encoding library resources compatible with the MCU architecture are relatively scarce. Moreover, the complete video encoding process involves cumbersome operations and complex logic, presenting a high technical barrier for developers. It should be specifically noted that this example project does not incorporate any standardised video encoding workflow. The final AVI format video file is generated by stitching together MJPG images captured frame by frame. Consequently, videos recorded using this approach may not achieve ideal standards in terms of image quality and smoothness. The core objective of this tutorial is to provide developers with a straightforward technical approach and practical method for implementing periodic recording and storage of short videos. Configure camera pins and parameters (JPEG format, SVGA resolution, PSRAM buffer, etc.) Initialise camera; if failed, output error code via serial port and terminate; if successful, mark camera as available Initialise SD card; detect card type (MMC/SDSC/SDHC); if no card present or initialisation failed, terminate; if successful, mark SD card as available Serial port prompts "Recording commences in 1 minute", indicating readiness When both camera and SD card are available, initiate video recording every 60 seconds Generate AVI filenames sequentially, creating/opening corresponding video files on SD card Record 10-second video segments by cyclically acquiring camera frame data and writing to file, then releasing frame buffer Upon completion, close the video file; serial port prompts "Saved successfully" with incremented video sequence number Delay to fill remaining minute duration, then await next recording cycle We have previously mastered the techniques for capturing camera images and understand the fundamental nature of moving video—composed of a continuous sequence of static frames. Based on this principle, this chapter will focus on a practical project: writing a programme to record a 10-second video clip every minute and automatically save the video file to a microSD card, thereby effortlessly accomplishing the periodic capture and local storage of video footage. As this instance will also utilise the camera functionality, it is necessary to verify that PSRAM is enabled prior to flashing. It is designed with a TFT color backlight display, paired with LoRa and GPS modules. It integrates the WiFi, Bluetooth, and LoRa communication standards commonly used in IoT, supports the 850-930MHz frequency band and LoRaWAN protocol, is compatible with Mesh networks, and meets the needs of scenarios such as smart cities and industrial control. Product Positioning: This product is primarily targeted at IoT engineers, smart hardware engineers, and open-source hardware enthusiasts, providing them with a hardware development platform for WiFi, Bluetooth, and LoRa communication technologies. It is an extensible Mesh development hardware platform for makers/developers with high demands, focusing on offline self-organizing network communication without public internet; This product is aimed at makers, hardware developers, and DIY enthusiasts; satisfying enthusiasts who want to modify the enclosure, attach external sensors, build gateways, or modify firmware through this product. It also targets college students and STEM education groups for wireless communication course experiments and course design. As well as hikers, mountaineers, trail runners, campers, and off-road vehicle teams; and emergency preparedness (Prepper) groups. This product features solar power and has built-in sensor chips, so it can be directly applied to research teams, small project integrators, field monitoring, search-and-rescue drills, and agricultural monitoring prototype validation; it is not intended for large-scale mass production, but rather for quickly building LoRa-Mesh prototypes and rapidly validating business logic. Program Introduction This demo program verifies the driver, partial refresh, and low-power sleep of the 2.13" GDEY0213B74 e-ink display (SSD1680 driven). The screen's physical resolution is 122×250, the program uses it in landscape mode as 250×122; frame buffer uses double buffering (current frame + previous frame), partial refresh only pushes the changed strip. LEFT / RIGHT to turn pages, each page full-screen refresh takes about 1.7s. On the REFRESH page, press UP / DOWN to change the counter value — only the progress bar changes. On the SLEEP page, press PRESS and the full screen goes black, after which only MENU can wake it. Main features include: INIT: Executes pin detection and reset timing, sends initialization sequence, displays measured time on screen; on power-on first probes panel type (after reset + SWRESET, if BUSY goes high within 300ms, it's determined to be an e-ink screen). REFRESH: Compares two refresh methods — partial refresh (0x22=0xFC non-flash waveform) vs full-screen refresh (0xD7). Counter and progress bar only refresh that one strip, displays measured time for both methods on screen. SLEEP: Enters deep sleep (0x10/0x01, approx. 1µA). Before entering, refreshes the entire screen to black as an "asleep" marker; after that only the MENU key can wake it (hardware reset + reinitialize), other keys are unresponsive. CLEAN: Clear screen mode, fills frame buffer with white then runs one full-screen refresh waveform, screen turns all white and stays blank. LEFT / RIGHT to leave. Refresh time measured: Full-screen refresh approx. 1718ms, partial refresh one strip approx. 363ms, initialization approx. 1837ms, clear screen approx. 1717ms. Auto-clear ghosting: Automatically inserts one full-screen refresh every 8 partial refreshes to suppress e-ink ghosting accumulation. Bottom right corner displays page number n/4, dynamic area on page fixed to one strip (Y=56, height 50), Mode / Count / PartN / Busy four items must refresh in the same strip. Program Introduction This demo program verifies the three-piece human-machine interaction: 6 buttons (MENU + joystick 5-direction), indicator LED, and buzzer. Unlike the blocking button library used by full firmware, this demo adopts fully non-blocking implementation — button scanning, LED flashing, and buzzer are all driven by main loop polling, non-blocking with each other, and not stuck by screen refresh. On power-on, it first flashes the LED twice and beeps twice. Then the screen displays the KEYS page. Use MENU to turn pages, UP / DOWN to switch four rhythms, the LED page indicator LED changes accordingly, the BUZZER page switches four alert tone modes, press any key to hear feedback tone. Main features include: KEYS: 6 buttons real-time display of physical state (IDLE / DOWN / LONG) and short press / long press cumulative count Debounce & Long Press Detection: timestamp debounce 20ms, long press threshold 800ms, after reaching the threshold generates a HOLD repeat event every 200ms LED: OFF / ON / SLOW (1 Hz) / FAST (5 Hz) four rhythms, UP / DOWN to switch (long press can switch continuously), screen displays half cycle and flash count BUZZER: OFF / KEY (button feedback single tone) / ALERT (long beep alert) / BEAT (beep-beep prompt tone) four modes, UP / DOWN to switch Button Assignment: MENU short press to next page (KEYS page only exit, because LEFT / RIGHT need to be kept as observed objects), MENU long press to clear all counts; LEFT / RIGHT only respond to short press, avoiding long press continuous page turning Any Key Feedback: In BUZZER = KEY mode, any button gives a short feedback tone (short press 40ms / long press 80ms) Power-on Default: LED = SLOW (1 Hz running indicator), BUZZER = KEY; before screen initialization, flash LED twice + two short beeps Buzzer uses hardware PWM drive (base frequency 2731 Hz), no CPU timer occupied Hardware Connection Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Performance KEYS LED BUZZER After flashing the firmware, you can view the actual results.

Program Introduction This demo program covers the complete battery chain flow: charging status read, voltage & power conversion, over-voltage/under-voltage protection, and controllability verification of the full board power domains. When USB is plugged in, the CHG page shows charging, changes to fully charged when done; unplugging USB shows not charging. The BATT page displays voltage within tens of mV of the multimeter measured value, power slowly decreases as it discharges; PROT page switches to SIM mode, use UP / DOWN to adjust simulated voltage across thresholds, can observe protection state trigger and recovery; PWR page press PRESS to hear feedback of Grove 5V domain on/off, the other three domains marked as FIX (not disconnectable). Main features include: CHG Charging Status: displays three states — charging / fully charged / not charging, with pin level and state change count BATT Voltage & Power: ADC raw code, voltage divider ratio, converted voltage, curve interpolated power, and draws discharge curve chart PROT Over/Under Voltage Protection: hysteresis protection state machine, supports REAL (measured voltage) and SIM (simulated voltage) two modes, PRESS to switch PWR Power Domain Management: lists controllability and current state of four power domains, PRESS to truly cut Grove 5V domain on/off, and gives whole board power consumption estimate Sampling Power-off: voltage divider chain has high-side P-MOS switch (Q8), BAT_ADC_CTR set high to connect, immediately pull low after sampling to avoid continuously consuming about 200µA Charging Status Correct Identification: CN3165 is open-drain output, pulled up to CHG_IND_VCC via LED + 10kΩ. This rail only has power when USB is plugged in; so it must be configured as INPUT_PULLUP to distinguish "not charging" from "floating". Power Non-linear Conversion: uses 12-point lithium battery discharge curve lookup table + piecewise interpolation, because 3.7–3.9V plateau region occupies about 50% capacity, linear conversion would be severely distorted. Protection Hysteresis: over-voltage 4250mV trigger / 4150mV recovery, under-voltage 3300mV trigger / 3450mV recovery, avoids repeated switching at critical points. Power Domain Truthfully Labeled: only Grove 5V domain on the whole board can truly be powered off; the three 3V3 domains LoRa / GNSS / Display are always powered by three-pin LDO without EN, can only rely on chip-level sleep, page clearly marks CUT / FIX. Hardware Connection Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable (need to plug in USB to observe charging status) Connect a lithium battery to observe voltage, power, and discharge curve; unplug USB to observe "not charging" determination Performance CHARGE BATTERY PROTECT POWER After flashing the firmware, you can view the actual results.

When installing Arduino libraries, there are usually two options available: online installation and offline installation. If a library requires offline installation, you must use the provided library files. For most libraries, users can easily search for and install them via the Arduino software’s online library manager. However, some open-source or custom libraries are not synchronised with the Arduino library manager and therefore cannot be obtained via an online search. In such cases, users must install these libraries manually using the offline method. As the library files for this product are already included in the compressed package for the sample program, there is no need to download any additional libraries.

All example programs have their own .ino files, which you can modify based on the source code to achieve the expected results. There are also pre-compiled .bin files that can be flashed directly with flash_download_tool. The .bin files ending with "merged" in each demo's "build" folder can be flashed directly.

Open the tool​ Open the Flash Download Tool; double-click the .exe file to access the main interface, as shown below: ChipType : Chip type: select according to the product type used WorkMode : Software mode: there are currently two modes — Develop mode and Factory mode — the differences are as follows: Develop : This mode uses the absolute path of the firmware and only supports flashing single-chip products. Factory : Since this mode uses relative paths, we recommend placing the firmware to be flashed in the "bin" folder at the same level as the .exe file; when the application is closed, the configuration is automatically saved locally. Factory : When opened, the interface is locked; you must click the "Lock Settings" button to enable editing. This prevents accidental mouse operations. LoadMode : The download interface supports UART and USB SPI Download interface​ The following are configuration instructions: Download Path Config : Include the firmware load path and download address, entered in hexadecimal format, e.g., 0x1000. SPI Flash Config SPI SPEED : SPI clock speed SPI MODE : SPI flash mode DETECTED INFO : Automatically detects flash and crystal oscillator information DoNotChgBin : If enabled, the original contents of the bin file will be flashed. If disabled, the settings will be updated and flashed according to the SPI SPEED and SPI MODE configuration on the interface. CombineBin button: You can bundle multiple firmware files selected in the download path configuration into a single firmware file. If DoNotChgBin is enabled, the files will be bundled as-is. If DoNotChgBin is not enabled, the firmware will be bundled according to the SPI SPEED and SPI MODE settings on the interface. Non-data areas between firmware files are filled with 0xff. The merged firmware is saved as .combine/target.bin; each click overwrites the previous version. Default button: Resets all SPI interface settings to default values Download Panel START : Start button STOP : Stop button ERASE : Full flash erase COM : Download serial port BAUD : Download baud rate Factory Multi-Download interface​ Factory : This mode uses relative paths, loading firmware by default from the bin directory in the tool directory for flashing. The Develop mode, however, uses absolute paths. The advantage of Factory mode is that once the firmware to be flashed is copied to the bin directory in the tool directory, it can be copied between factory computers without path issues. When Factory mode is enabled, LockSettings is enabled by default when the tool starts. Once enabled, neither the firmware paths nor the SPI flash config can be modified. preventing configuration errors caused by accidental changes by production line personnel. (Factory managers who need to make configurations can click LockSettings to unlock.) The download path config and SPI flash config settings on the FactoryMultiDownload interface are basically the same as those on the SPIDownload interface. Please refer to SPIDownload Interface, and make sure you configure the serial port number and baud rate for each channel separately. Chip Info Dump interface​ Device : Select the serial port number and baud rate of the relevant device. Read Flash: Select the start address and the size of the data to read from flash. This option is set only when reading flash. Function Description Chip Info: Reads the chip model, flash ID, and flash status register values; the data is displayed directly on the software interface. Read Flash: Reads data from flash. The read data is stored in a generated bin file with the format: "chip MAC + read data start address + read data length + read time". Read eFuse: Reads the contents of the chip's eFuse; this function is the same as ESPTOOL's summary command. The read data is stored in a generated text file with the format "chip MAC + read time".

Overview​ This demo program is designed to verify the basic functions of the OLED on the W15. After powering on, the program initializes the OLED and then loops as follows: Text display demo Basic graphics demo (rectangle, circle, line) Simple animation demo (moving square, breathing circle) Progress bar 0-100% Hardware​ Development board: ESP32-S3 LR2021 development kit (W15) OLED: I2C, SDA=GPIO5, SCL=GPIO4, RST=GPIO38 Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ The OLED screen will sequentially display text, basic shapes (rectangle, circle, line), animations (moving square, breathing circle), and a progress bar. After flashing the firmware, you can view the actual results

Overview​ Uses the Adafruit_NeoPixel library to drive the RGB LED connected to GPIO48, implementing basic color cycling, fast blinking, smooth color transitions, and breathing light effects. Main features include: Initializes the single on-board RGB LED using RGB color format and an 800 kHz communication rate. Cycles through the three primary colors—red, green, and blue—switching automatically every 500 milliseconds Provides a fast six-color blinking effect with red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, and magenta alternating Supports a smooth warm-yellow brightness gradient, with brightness gradually increasing from 0 to 255 and then decreasing back to 0 Creates a cyan breathing light effect, with the light blinking in a slow, rhythmic pattern All light effects are displayed in an auto-cycling manner, with the current display state output via the serial port Provides the standard setColor() function for easily customizing any RGB color Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Performance The built-in LED on the board will cycle through four different light effects After flashing the firmware, you can view the actual results:

Overview​ This program demonstrates the Wi-Fi scanning function of the W15. At startup, it sets the Wi-Fi to STA mode and periodically scans nearby 2.4GHz Wi-Fi networks. After each scan completes, it outputs the network list via the serial port, including: SSID (network name) RSSI (received signal strength indicator) Encryption type Channel number The program automatically repeats the scan every 5 seconds, allowing you to monitor changes in the surrounding Wi-Fi environment in real time. Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ Open the serial monitor at a baud rate of 115200 View all Wi-Fi information detected by the device

Overview​ This demonstrates the LoRa wireless transceiver function of the W15 development board, supporting one-key switching between transmit and receive modes, and flexible frequency switching, and an OLED display showing status and data in real time. It can run independently without connecting to a computer. Main features include: At startup, the device defaults to LoRa receive mode, continuously monitoring wireless data over the air Short-press the BOOT button to switch between frequency bands (868MHz/915MHz/2.4GHz, etc.). Long-press the BOOT button to switch between receive (RX) and transmit (TX) modes In TX mode, a data packet containing a transmission sequence number is automatically sent every second In RX mode, received packets are automatically parsed, displaying signal strength (RSSI) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) The OLED screen displays the following in real time: operating mode, frequency band, transmit/receive counts, signal strength, and the latest message The serial port synchronously outputs transmission and reception logs, data content, and RSSI/SNR parameters for easy debugging Pre-configured standard LoRa parameters ensure reliable communication with other LoRa devices. Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ Actual appearance

Overview​ The on-board BOOT button (GPIO0) is used to detect short and long presses, with the RGB LED providing visual feedback; the system also includes button debouncing and safe interrupt handling. Main features include: Uses an interrupt-based approach for button detection, ensuring fast response without occupying main loop resources Built-in 50-millisecond button debouncing effectively prevents false triggering caused by voltage fluctuations Automatically detects two operation modes: short press of less than 1000 milliseconds and long press of 1000 milliseconds or more On short press, the RGB LED cycles through eight colors (red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta, white, and off). On long press, the RGB LED automatically switches to a cyan breathing light effect; long-press again to exit Real-time serial output of key type, press duration, cumulative count, and current LED color The button uses an internal pull-up configuration, requiring no external circuitry; just use the on-board BOOT button. The interrupt service routine (ISR) is decorated with IRAM_ATTR to ensure running stability Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ Open the serial monitor Press the BOOT button to switch the LED on and off After flashing the firmware, you can view the actual results:

Overview​ This project demonstrates the ADC analog acquisition capability of the W15. It periodically reads data from two ADC channels (GPIO1 and GPIO2), reduces noise by averaging multiple samples, and outputs the results to the serial port as voltage values and percentages. Main features include: Configures 12-bit ADC resolution with 11 dB attenuation (approx. 0–3.3 V range) Dual-channel sampling with averaging filter Raw value, voltage value, and percentage display Estimates battery voltage based on voltage divider assumptions, outputting charge status (fully charged / normal / low / needs charging) Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ Dual-channel ADC sampling (10-point averaging) Raw value, voltage, and percentage display Battery voltage estimation and status assessment

Overview​ By powering external sensors, initializing the I2C bus, scanning all devices on the bus, and providing a framework for reading common sensor data such as temperature, humidity, and pressure, the system can quickly identify and integrate various I2C sensors. Main features include: Controls the VEXT power supply to power external I²C sensors, ensuring proper hardware operation Initializes the I2C bus (SDA: 17 / SCL: 18), supporting the standard 100 kHz communication rate Automatically scans all slave addresses on the I2C bus, identifying common devices (OLED, AHT20, SHT31, BMP280, etc.) Provides a framework for reading temperature, humidity, and pressure sensor data, facilitating integration with real-world sensor libraries Encapsulates utility functions for reading and writing generic I2C registers, which can be used directly in various I2C device drivers Periodically outputs sensor data; supports polling every 2 seconds Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable If you need to attach a sensor, you can use this program to check whether the sensor is correctly connected. Expected result​

Overview​ This program implements timer wake-up, GPIO button wake-up, and a combination of both wake-up sources. Upon waking, it displays a visual signal via the RGB LED while turning off external power to reduce power consumption. Main features include: Uses RTC memory to store the variable recording the number of system boots; the data remains unchanged during deep sleep Automatically detects and prints the wake-up reason (timer, GPIO button, first boot, or reset) Supports a 10-second automatic wake-up timer Supports manual wake-up via GPIO0 (BOOT button) Adopts a dual wake-up source mode combining timer and button; the device wakes up when either condition is met Upon waking, the RGB LED flashes blue three times as an indicator Turns off the RGB LED before entering sleep mode to optimize power efficiency Outputs complete sleep status, wake-up information, and statistics via the serial port After deep sleep, the program restarts from setup() loop() function is never executed Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​

Overview​ This program demonstrates the data transmission and reception capabilities of a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi TCP server on the W15 development board. After connecting to a router, the device sets up a TCP server and waits for a client (such as a network debugging assistant) to connect, enabling bidirectional data pass-through, echo testing, and status monitoring. Main features include: Connects to the specified 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network in STA mode, automatically obtains an IP address, and supports automatic reconnection Sets up a TCP server on port 8080, waiting for remote client connections Supports a single client connection; automatically sends a welcome message once connected Receives client data and echoes it back unchanged for bidirectional pass-through testing Automatically sends a statistics heartbeat packet to the client every 10 seconds, containing send/receive counts and Wi-Fi signal strength The OLED screen displays the following information in real time: Wi-Fi status, local IP address, client IP address, number of packets sent and received, and the latest message Complete serial output of connection information, sent and received data, signal strength, and network parameters Automatically turns on VEXT to power the OLED, completing screen initialization and real-time refresh Automatically restores the server state on connection failure and keeps monitoring Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable If you cannot connect to Wi-Fi, you can attach a Wi-Fi antenna to the board Expected result​ After the program runs, you can view the IP address assigned when connecting to Wi-Fi, the TCP client's IP address, and the data received on the screen. Real-time output of connection status, received data content, and transmitted data length Displays Wi-Fi connection details and statistics For easy debugging and monitoring of the program's running status Use a TCP connection tool to establish a connection and send messages, and check whether the data is transmitted successfully After the connection is established, the device's serial port displays a message that the client has connected. Sent successfully

Overview​ This program demonstrates the BLE Bluetooth scanning function of the W15 development board. It automatically searches for nearby Bluetooth devices and displays the device name, MAC address, and signal strength (RSSI) in real time on the OLED screen. It runs independently without pairing with a phone. Main features include: Initializes the BLE device and enables active scanning mode; sets the duration of each scan cycle to 3 seconds Automatically detects and records nearby BLE devices, caching information for up to 20 devices For unnamed Bluetooth devices, the last 8 digits of the MAC address are automatically used as the device identifier Scan results are displayed on the OLED screen in pages (four devices per page) with automatic page scrolling Real-time display of scan cycle, number of detected devices, current page number, device name, and RSSI signal strength The complete scan list (serial number, name, MAC, RSSI) is output via the serial port for easy debugging and viewing Automatically turns on the VEXT power supply for the OLED, completing screen initialization and status refresh A "Please wait" prompt is displayed on the screen during scanning, improving user experience After the scan completes, the results are automatically cleared and the next round begins. Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ After power-on, the OLED display initializes and BLE scanning begins. During scanning, the screen displays "Scanning"; a complete scan cycle takes 3 seconds. Scan results are displayed in a paged scrolling view on the OLED screen, with four devices shown per page. Displays device name and signal strength; for unidentified devices, the MAC address is displayed. If no devices are found, the screen displays a prompt that no BLE devices were discovered. Device information is output to the serial port, and scanning automatically restarts after each cycle completes.

Overview​ This program demonstrates the web-based remote control function of the W15 development board over Wi-Fi. After the device connects to Wi-Fi, it starts a web server; users can then Access the device's IP address via a web browser to remotely control the OLED display, adjust brightness, switch the RGB light on and off, and view the device's running status in real time. Main features include: Connects to the specified Wi-Fi network, starts the web server on port 80, and displays the access IP on the OLED screen. The web interface provides a graphical control panel supporting remote switching between three display shapes: square, circle, and triangle. Supports custom text input via the web page, displayed in real time in the center of the OLED screen Equipped with a brightness slider allowing you to adjust the OLED contrast (10–255), with changes taking effect immediately Supports remote control of the on-board green RGB LED, with the on/off status displayed synchronously on the web page Provides a screen clear button that clears the OLED display and returns to the standby screen with a single click The web page displays Wi-Fi signal strength (RSSI), device uptime, current display mode, and LED status in real time Built-in automatic reconnection mechanism ensures stable and uninterrupted remote control during Wi-Fi disconnections Automatically turns on the VEXT power supply for the OLED, completing screen initialization and display refresh The website features a green tech design, optimized for viewing on various devices, including computers and phones. Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable If you have confirmed the SSID and password are correct but still cannot connect via Wi-Fi, you need to attach an antenna to the Wi-Fi antenna connector on the back of the board. Expected result​ After entering the SSID and password, the device displays the IP address once the connection succeeds. You can then access the corresponding URL via a web browser. After the request succeeds, the corresponding control buttons and other elements will appear on the web page Shape display: Square Shape display: Circle Custom text Control: RGB LED Control: CLEAR OLED Device status: The web page displays Wi-Fi signal strength (RSSI), device uptime, current display mode, and LED status in real time

Overview​ The Bluetooth + LoRa wireless gateway function of the W15 development board allows a phone to control LoRa data transmission via BLE and relay the received LoRa data back to the phone via BLE, achieving bidirectional transparent transmission and enabling wireless relaying without a network connection. Main features include: Initializes the BLE server as a device named W15-Gateway, waiting for a mobile phone to connect The phone sends data via BLE; the device automatically receives it and forwards it through the LoRa module Monitors LoRa wireless data in real time and automatically pushes it to your phone via BLE upon receipt The OLED screen displays the following information in real time: BLE connection status, LoRa transmit and receive counts, the latest message, and status information Built-in LoRa parameter configuration: 915 MHz frequency band, 125 kHz bandwidth, SF7, sync word 0x34 Synchronous serial output of BLE and LoRa transmission and reception logs for easy debugging Powers the OLED, completing screen initialization and status refresh Automatically restarts advertising after the BLE connection is dropped, ensuring the gateway remains available at all times Data flow​ Hardware connection​ Connect the board to the computer with a USB cable Expected result​ After power-on, the OLED display initializes, and the LoRa module and BLE service start automatically. BLE advertises under the name W15-Gateway, waiting for a phone to connect Once the phone connects via BLE, the OLED display shows "BLE connected," and the gateway enters standby mode The phone sends data via BLE; the W15 receives it and transmits it via LoRa Upon receiving LoRa data, the W15 automatically passes it back to the phone via BLE The OLED display updates the BLE status, LoRa transmit/receive counts, and the latest message in real time Synchronous serial printing of BLE and LoRa transmitted/received data and status information After the BLE connection is dropped, the device automatically resumes advertising, while LoRa continues monitoring the signal You can search for and download the nRF Connect app in the major mobile app stores; this app allows your phone to search for and connect to Bluetooth devices. documents.t: The LR2021 RF Transceiver Module is an ultra-compact embedded development module for IoT developers, makers and small electronics manufacturers, combining Semtech's 4th-generation LoRa RF transceiver LR2021 with the ESP32-S3 Mini Module. The ESP32-S3 sub-module is built around a high-performance dual-core 32-bit LX7 MCU (up to 240 MHz), with an on-board NPU, 16 MB Flash, 8 MB PSRAM, Wi-Fi 802.11b/g/n and Bluetooth 5.0, 32 GPIOs and multiple high-speed buses. It ships with a temperature sensor and 6-axis IMU, measuring 24.54 mm × 17.78 mm × 4.50 mm. The LR2021 sub-module is a 4th-gen high-performance multi-band LoRa transceiver supporting long-range LoRa communication and FLRC high-speed transmission up to 2.6 Mbps. It covers Sub-GHz (868/915 MHz) and 2.4 GHz ISM bands, with receive sensitivity up to -141.5 dBm and output power up to +22 dBm. Native LoRaWAN® support and SPI interface for seamless mating with the W11 dev board.

The LR2021 RF Transceiver Module tightly integrates the ESP32-S3's computing power + dual Wi-Fi/Bluetooth + rich peripherals with the LR2021's long-range LoRa wireless link into an ultra-compact embedded combo module for IoT developers, makers, and small electronics manufacturers. While retaining a tiny footprint, it delivers strong edge computing, flexible multi-protocol wireless connectivity and low-power operation — ideal for space-constrained smart devices and IoT applications that need both Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and LoRa links. Target Audience：IoT application developers, makers and DIY enthusiasts, educational institutions and students, smart monitoring equipment manufacturers, industrial IoT solution providers, portable electronics design teams.

The W16 combo module combines the LR2021's long-range LoRa communication capability with the ESP32-S3's local edge computing and Wi-Fi/Bluetooth connectivity. It supports point-to-point, star and LoRa-Mesh networking, enabling dual-channel data transfer: long-range LoRa backhaul + Wi-Fi cloud upload. Industrial IoT Monitoring Key Function: Long-range LoRa + ESP32-S3 edge computing + multi-sensor interface Industrial field sensor data acquisition (temperature/humidity, pressure, liquid level, vibration); factory equipment status monitoring, alerts and remote data backhaul. The ESP32-S3 performs local data pre-processing and edge AI analysis, while LoRa handles long-distance backhaul — suitable for wide-area deployment in workshops and plants where cabling is difficult. Smart Water / Smart Gas Key Function: Long-range LoRa + Wi-Fi configuration + low-power modes Wireless water meters, wireless gas meters, pipeline pressure monitoring terminals; well and underground network data acquisition. Long battery life, no cabling needed; enables automated meter reading and anomaly alerts. Wi-Fi for short-range parameter configuration, Bluetooth for mobile APP connection, LoRa for long-distance data backhaul. Smart Agriculture Key Function: Long-range LoRa + ESP32-S3 local processing + multi-sensor expansion Farmland soil moisture, temperature/humidity and light monitoring; greenhouse environment control; long-range data collection in mountain orchards; livestock farming environment monitoring. The ESP32-S3 ships with on-board temperature/humidity and inertial sensors and can be expanded with external soil-moisture and fertigation sensors for long-term battery-powered field deployment. Smart City Infrastructure Key Function: Long-range LoRa + Wi-Fi hotspot + GPIO control Smart street-light control, manhole-cover status monitoring, waterlogging detection, waste-sorting equipment status reporting; wide-area low-rate city IoT data collection. The ESP32-S3 can act as a Wi-Fi hotspot for nearby devices while LoRa handles long-range node networking. Security & Emergency Key Function: LoRa ad-hoc network + ESP32-S3 edge computing + multi-sensor interface Outdoor intrusion detection, wireless alarm sensors, emergency call terminals; long-range alert transmission. When public networks are down (earthquakes, floods, fires), LoRa ad-hoc networks can quickly set up temporary communications, with the ESP32-S3 coordinating all nodes. Portable Battery-Powered Terminals Key Function: Low-power deep sleep + Li-ion management + dual LoRa/Wi-Fi Field data loggers, handheld wireless collectors, remote-control terminals.
